transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-25
Start: 16:00 UTC
Scheduled duration: 45 min (actual 46)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Sophie Li (Redwood Solutions), Liam O'Connor (Everest, Head of ML), Priya Desai (Everest, Platform), Daniel Hart (Everest, Procurement)

Auto-generated summary: Cost economics deep-dive; agreed to pilot and requested security docs and cost spreadsheet. Transcript quality: medium (some transcription errors).

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you carving time. quick intros?
[00:10] Liam O'Connor: yeah hi liam here, head of ML at everest, we run a bunch of inference workloads for research and prod pricing models.
[00:17] Priya Desai: priya, platform eng - we own deployment and budgeting for infra.
[00:21] Daniel Hart: daniel, procurement - here to understand contracting and timeline.
[00:25] Ravi Patel: ravi, solutions eng at redwood, i'll cover perf and batching questions.
[00:30] Maya Chen: cool. goal today is to dig into unit economics - per-token pricing, what batching/caching levers you have, and how hosted vs dedicated vs private would affect cost and latency.

[01:05] Liam: brief context: we're revisiting inference costs. currently spinning on-prem GPUs and some cloud endpoints. our big worry is unpredictable token cost with spikes and the seq lengths are wide - sometimes 128 tokens, sometimes 2k for research. target is under $X per 1k tokens for prod but we need to see realistic numbers.

[01:40] Priya: also constraints: data can't leave our VPC for some models (PII), so we're considering private for those. but for general purpose assistants hosted would be okay if we can cap spend.

[02:05] Maya: makes sense. quick primer: hosted is simplest (Redwood API) with predictable published per-token units and quotas; dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and better unit costs at scale because of committed capacity; private gives you the most control for residency/compliance but involves fixed platform fees and infra ops.

[02:40] Ravi: on the tech side, two big cost levers - batching and KV/prefix caching. batching boosts throughput (amortizes kernel overhead) but increases tail latency for single-request flows. KV cache/prefix caching can make repeated context cheap - for chatty conversational workloads we often see big drops in tokens per response.

[03:10] Liam: can you quantify? like, what % cost reduction with batching?

[03:15] Ravi: rough heuristics: with continuous batching and typical small chat messages (<=256 tokens), batching can reduce cost per token by 20-50% depending on QPS distribution and model. for larger sequences the benefit shrinks. caching sometimes reduces effective token generation by 30%+ for repetitive prompts. important caveat: your prompt mix matters.

[03:58] Priya: what about KV cache miss penalties - does it add latency?

[04:05] Ravi: miss is mostly a cold compute path; hit is very cheap because you reuse KV state. miss can add a bit of setup time but not huge. also quantization affects both throughput and quality; int8/4 quantization saves memory and increases throughput but may regress on certain tasks.

[04:40] Liam: talk to me about pricing units - do you charge input+output tokens? peak vs amortized?

[04:47] Maya: standard is per-token billing covering generation and prompt tokens (input+output); for hosted we publish token rates per model family; dedicated often has effective lower unit price depending on commit and utilization; private is license/platform fee + infra cost so unit economics depend on your utilization rate.

[05:20] Daniel: example - if we run 5M tokens/day, what's ballpark monthly spend hosted vs dedicated?

[05:30] Maya: quick ballpark (very rough): hosted for one of our mid-tier models might be $0.002 per 1k tokens - actually this is illustrative, exact rates depend on model. at 5M tokens/day that's 150M tokens/month -> multiply by per-1k rate gives rough $300/month at $0.002 per 1k? (note: example numbers on call, will send spreadsheet). but realistic numbers vary, and with high QPS/dedicated you can get appreciable discounts via reserved capacity.

[06:10] Priya: i think there's a math mismatch - check the units, 5M tokens/day -> 150M/month. at $0.002 per 1k tokens that's $300, yes that's low; i think enterprise models or larger can be multiple x. we need a model-led spreadsheet.

[06:33] Ravi: yeah sorry these on-the-fly numbers; we'll send detailed cost model with scenarios: varying seq lengths, cache hit rates, batching profiles, and dedicated commit tiers.

[06:50] Liam: can you share how batching config looks - do you need changes to client?

[06:57] Ravi: no, our runtime handles continuous batching server-side for hosted/dedicated. for best results you can control max latency SLO and batching window. on private deployments we ship the same runtime but you manage config. so little to no client changes required beyond setting route and SLO.

[07:25] Priya: what about cold starts and autoscaling on dedicated? we have daily traffic spikes.

[07:32] Maya: dedicated supports burst capacity and autoscale policies. for spikes low-latency SLOs we recommend a base pool sized for baseline plus a small burst buffer and autoscale triggers. costs are mostly from reserved capacity; bursts can be billed differently depending on contract.

[08:00] Liam: security - we have models that can't leave our network. private option required for those, but unclear on overall economics. what does private price include?

[08:10] Sophie Li: private includes a platform fee (annual license) for the private control plane, plus support/ops tier options; infra cost (GPU, networking) is separate. we provide connectors for KMS/HSM and audit logs; compliance docs: SOC2, ISO we can share.

[08:35] Priya: does private support our existing KMS and SSO?

[08:40] Sophie: yes - SAML/SSO and KMS integrations are supported, though on-prem installs have some additional configuration. we'll send the ops checklist.

[09:00] Daniel: procurement question - if we start with hosted pilot and then move to dedicated/private, how does contract flow work? do credits apply?

[09:10] Maya: typically we do a hosted pilot (short-term), and if you move to dedicated we credit pilot usage toward new commit depending on timing. procurement specifics we'll work with you on.

[09:30] Liam: okay pilot - what's a realistic pilot to validate cost econ? 1 week with typical traffic?

[09:36] Ravi: 1-2 weeks is enough if you share representative traffic and token distributions. we run benchmarks capturing latency, cost per token under different batching windows, and cache hit rates. for your case we'd run both short-chats and long-seq tests.

[10:00] Priya: what telemetry will you need from us?

[10:05] Ravi: token distribution, QPS over time, 95/99 latency SLO targets, and examples of common prompts. Priya, if you can share the last 90 days token histogram that's ideal.

[10:20] Priya: will do.

[10:25] Liam: any quality regressions when moving to quantized models? we've seen hallucinations with aggressive quant.

[10:33] Ravi: it's model-dependent. int8 often minimal regression on many tasks; int4 and some post-training quant strategies can introduce regressions. we recommend evaluation harnesses for your critical prompts - Redwood Optimize provides quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to prompt sets.

[11:00] Maya: another trade-off - if you pin older model versions to save costs, you might see quality drift vs newer ones; we support rollouts and A/B to test.

[11:15] Liam: competition - we've talked to Anthropic and OpenAI. how are you differentiated on cost?

[11:22] Maya: we focus on runtime efficiency and production levers - batching, caching, KV management, and routing. customers often see better unit economics for heavier throughput workloads because of our runtime and reserved capacity options. we also provide transparent cost breakdowns per-token and token-per-route analytics.

[11:45] Daniel: on invoicing and metering - do we get token-level breakdowns?

[11:50] Sophie: yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level cost breakdown by route/model/token-type and retention options; we can increase retention for audits as an add-on.

[12:05] Priya: ok, two more technicals: how do you handle KV cache for multi-tenant hosted env? is data siloed?

[12:13] Ravi: KV cache is tenant-scoped; for hosted customers we guarantee logical isolation and encryption at rest. for dedicated/private you have stronger isolation guarantees since you own or reserve the pool.

[12:35] Liam: any gotchas with prefix caching and variable seqs? sometimes our prompts vary slightly and cache hit rate drops.

[12:42] Ravi: yep that's normal. we use fuzzy prefix matching and canonicalization heuristics to boost hit rates, but application-level prompt engineering helps a lot - canonicalize system prompts, strip ephemeral tokens.

[13:00] Priya: what's the SLA for dedicated?

[13:04] Maya: SLA tiers exist; standard is 99.9% with latency targets depending on model family and commit level; enterprise customers can opt for higher SLAs. we'll share the SLA doc.

[13:20] Daniel: procurement timeline - we ideally want to be in pilot within 2 weeks and procurement in 4-6 weeks. is that realistic?

[13:27] Maya: yes, pilot can start fast; procurement timeline for dedicated/private depends on legal review but 4-6 weeks is common.

[13:35] Liam: what logs/trace data do you provide so we can reconcile spend?

[13:40] Sophie: detailed usage logs, token counts per request, per-route analytics, and tracing hooks. all available via console and exports to S3.

[14:00] Priya: please include an example cost sheet with scenarios: low, medium, high utilization; impact of 30% cache hit; batching windows 10ms/50ms/100ms.

[14:12] Maya: will do.

[14:20] Liam: any advice on starting with mixed approach - hosted for non-sensitive, private for PII?

[14:25] Maya: that's a common pattern. we recommend starting hosted for general features to iterate fast and then migrate sensitive flows to private when you're ready; routing policies can split by route so it's seamless.

[14:45] Daniel: compliance docs? can you share SOC2 + encryption details?

[14:50] Sophie: yes - we'll share SOC2 report, encryption at rest/in transit, and an ops checklist for private.

[15:05] Liam: are there any hidden costs - egress, storage for KV cache?

[15:12] Ravi: egress can be billed by underlying infra in private setups; on hosted we bake typical egress into pricing but large media transfers would be separate. KV cache storage is minimal relative to model weights but we'll show numbers.

[15:30] Priya: curious about per-token metering accuracy - rounding, sampling?

[15:35] Sophie: tokenization is deterministic; we meter input+output tokens. we publish tokenizer versions; for reconciliation we can provide hashes and request IDs.

[16:00] Liam: ok, let's recap next steps.

[16:05] Maya: recap: we will send cost model spreadsheet with scenarios, SOC2 + security deck, and a proposed 1-week hosted pilot plan to collect metrics; ravi will draft pilot steps; priya will send token histograms; daniel will share procurement timeline.

[16:25] Daniel: i'll follow up with PO process details.

[16:30] Priya: i'll send usage histograms by tomorrow.

[16:33] Liam: thanks all.

[16:35] Maya: great - i'll email the attachments and schedule follow-up for next week.

[16:40] Call ends.

Notes: transcription contains occasional errors (e.g., "KV cash" vs "KV cache", "Sam L" for SAML). Action items captured above.
